claims.text: Most college students actively use social media on a smartphone for more than three hours daily for socializing, entertainment, and education.
Moderate and goal-directed social media use is positively correlated with collaboration.
Moderate and goal-directed social media use is positively correlated with academic motivation.
Compulsive and obsessive social media use causes academic risks.
Compulsive and obsessive social media use causes psychological risks.
Constant access to idealized images of peers stimulates upward social comparison.
Constant access to idealized images of peers leads to higher levels of anxiety and stress.
Constant access to idealized images of peers leads to poor psychological well-being.
Digital task-switching is not related to learning.
Long periods of time spent online are linked with cognitive distraction and time substitution.
Long periods of time spent online are linked with late assignments.
Long periods of time spent online are linked with lower grade point average.

evidence.description: Survey results show that most college students are actively using social media daily on a smartphone for more than three hours with a view to socializing, entertainment, and education.
Statistical analysis of survey responses found that moderate and goal-directed social media use is positively correlated with collaboration.
Statistical analysis showed moderate and goal-directed social media use is positively correlated with academic motivation.
Survey analysis revealed that compulsive and obsessive social media use causes serious academic risks.
Survey analysis revealed that compulsive and obsessive social media use causes serious psychological risks.
Results indicate constant access to idealized images of peers stimulates social comparison among university students.
Constant access to idealized images of peers was found to lead to higher levels of anxiety and stress.
Constant access to idealized images of peers was reported to lead to poor psychological well-being.
Analysis demonstrated that digital task-switching is not related to learning.
Long periods of time spent online were found to be linked with cognitive distraction and time substitution.
Long periods of time spent online were linked with late assignments among respondents.
Statistical findings linked long periods of time spent online with lower grade point average.

methodologies.name: Descriptive survey methodology using stratified random sampling
methodologies.description: Questionnaires assessing social media usage, subjective well-being, and academic performance were administered to 331 undergraduate and graduate students from various faculties at the University of Sargodha and analyzed using SPSS.
datasets: Survey of 331 undergraduate and graduate students at the University of Sargodha
